text.p: A senior U.S. official, in a video-conference with anti-government protest leaders in Belgrade, on Wednesday praised their continued peaceful demonstrations.

"It is a tribute to the citizens of Serbia ... that you have brought so peacefully your expression to the streets day after day and shown ... you will not be denied your democratic rights," Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck said in a communications hookup from Washignton.

"We salute you and we recognise how challenging it is to press forward for your rights and for democracy. But you are doing it with great courage and the fact that you are doing it peacefully is what makes it so significant because that is the essence of the democratic process," he added.

Separately, the editor of Serbia's main independent radio station -- B92 -- faulted the United States for not giving more support to Serbian democratic forces and said Serbians were not convinced that Washington was on their side.
The editor, Veran Matic, said he did not believe massive streets protests in Serbia would result in the overthrow of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
But he stressed that the fate of democracy movements in Croatia and Serbia would go a long way toward determining whether peace in Bosnia succeeds or fails.

Shattuck, top U.S. policymaker on human rights, discussed Serbia with student leaders and opposition politicians involved in nearly three weeks of anti-government protests sparked when Belgrade invalidated a local election the opposition claimed to have won.
The video-conference linking Washington and Belgrade was arranged by Internews, a non-profit organisation that promotes independent media and alternative media worldwide.

Matic, whose radio station was shutdown briefly by Milosevic, spoke with reporters at a meeting arranged by the Open Society Institute, part of the foundation established by George Soros, the billionaire businessman and philanthropist.

Matic said he was in the U.S. capital to explain that "there are other democratic forces in Serbia who could be much better guarantors of the (U.S.-negotiated Bosnia) peace (deal) than Milosevic is or could be ever."
"It was a big mistake that the United States did not support the democratic movement in Serbia and that it could be counterproductive for peace in the whole region," he said.
He said there was a very strong popular push and desire for democracy and an independent media in Serbia but for a long time "this was ignored."
Matic and many experts believe Washington hesitated to fault Milosevic's authoritarianism because it depended on him as a key signer of the Bosnia peace deal.

In recent weeks, however, the United States has sided firmly with the protestors, warning Milosevic not to use force against them, cutting contacts with Milosevic, threatening to reimpose economic sanctions on Serbia and enlisting European allies in this campaign.
Asked if the United States was perceived in Serbia as being on the side of the opposition, Matic said "there is this ambiguous or ambivalent double-feeling."
The United States "has reacted (to the protests) much more strongly than the European Union ... but people trust much less the U.S.," he said.
Several of the students in the video-conference expressed displeasure with American news reports suggesting many of the protestors are nationalists, not democrats.
